title: Indian Contract Act, 1872 — Section 73 (Compensation for loss or damage caused by breach of contract)

content.overview: Section 73 provides compensation for loss or damage caused by breach where the loss naturally arose in the usual course of things or was of a kind the parties knew, when contracting, was likely to result. It excludes remote and indirect loss. Its Explanation requires the means that existed to remedy the inconvenience caused by non-performance to be taken into account. The statutory text and illustrations have been checked against the official India Code Act PDF; current-amendment status and case-law treatment have not been independently certified in this pass.

sections.heading: Statutory trigger and causation
sections.body: Start with a contract, a breach, and loss or damage caused by that breach. Section 73 is not a guarantee of every claimed amount: connect each head of loss to the breach and support it with facts and evidence.

sections.heading: Two statutory routes to recoverable loss
sections.body: The section covers loss or damage that (1) naturally arose in the usual course of things from the breach, or (2) was of a kind the parties knew, when they made the contract, was likely to result from the breach. Identify which route supports each claimed head of loss and what facts establish it.

sections.heading: Remote and indirect loss excluded
sections.body: Section 73 expressly excludes compensation for remote and indirect loss sustained by reason of the breach. The analysis should distinguish the loss caused by the breach from a more remote consequence and explain the connection rather than simply label the claim 'direct' or 'remote'.

sections.heading: Explanation: means of remedying the inconvenience
sections.body: When estimating loss or damage, the statutory Explanation requires the means that existed to remedy the inconvenience caused by non-performance to be taken into account. Consider available alternatives and their terms on the evidence; do not state an abstract mitigation rule without applying the facts.

sections.heading: Statutory illustrations and measure
sections.body: The Act illustrates ordinary market-difference measures for goods or a ship, expenses caused by arranging substitute carriage, repair costs for defective work, and limits on a claimed downstream contract loss where the relevant special contract had not been communicated. Apply the specific illustration only where the facts genuinely match it.

sections.heading: Separate related provisions
sections.body: Section 73 addresses compensation for loss caused by breach and also extends its rule to failure to discharge an obligation resembling one created by contract. Section 74 separately addresses a sum or penalty stipulated for breach; section 75 addresses compensation after rightful rescission. Identify the actual statutory basis before calculating relief.

sections.heading: Proof and application checklist
sections.body: For each head of loss, record the contractual obligation, breach, causal chain, amount and supporting documents; identify whether the loss naturally arose or was within the parties' knowledge when contracting; test remoteness; and account for available remedial means under the Explanation.

examples.title: Market difference for undelivered goods
examples.body: The Act illustrates a seller who fails to deliver goods. The buyer's measure is the amount, if any, by which the contract price falls short of the price for which goods of like quality could have been obtained at the relevant delivery time.

examples.title: Substitute carriage and avoidable inconvenience
examples.body: The Act illustrates a ship that does not arrive for a planned cargo. If the other party obtains suitable alternative conveyance on equally advantageous terms but incurs trouble and expense, the illustration allows compensation for that trouble and expense.

examples.title: Uncommunicated downstream contract
examples.body: The Act illustrates a machinery delivery breach where the buyer also loses a third-party contract that had not been communicated to the supplier when contracting. The illustration distinguishes the replacement-cost difference from the downstream compensation paid to the third party.

examples.title: Defective repair work
examples.body: The Act illustrates repairs performed contrary to the contract. The stated measure is the cost of making the repairs conform to the contract.

hypotheticals.question: A supplier delivers goods late and the market price has fallen. What should be established?
hypotheticals.analysis: Identify the agreed delivery date, breach, the market price at the time the goods ought to have been delivered, the actual loss and supporting market evidence. The statutory market-difference illustration may assist if the facts align.

hypotheticals.question: A buyer claims lost profits from a separate contract after the seller's breach. Is the full amount automatically recoverable?
hypotheticals.analysis: No automatic conclusion follows from the claim alone. Establish the parties' knowledge at contract formation, the causal chain and evidence of loss; test whether the loss is remote or indirect and consider the Act's illustration concerning an uncommunicated downstream contract.

hypotheticals.question: A party had an available alternative that would have reduced the consequences of non-performance. How is it relevant?
hypotheticals.analysis: Section 73's Explanation directs that available means of remedying the inconvenience be taken into account when estimating loss. Establish what alternative existed, its timing and terms, and the evidence about whether it could reasonably have addressed the inconvenience.

illustrations: Section 73 illustration (a): for undelivered goods, compare the contract price with the price obtainable for goods of like quality at the time they ought to have been delivered.
Section 73 illustration (b): where substitute carriage was available on equally advantageous terms, the illustration recognises trouble and expense incurred in arranging it.

Section 73 illustration (i): where a carrier's unreasonable delay causes a mill to lose a profitable government contract, the illustration distinguishes average profits lost during the delay from loss sustained through the uncommunicated government contract.
Section 73 illustration (f): where repairs do not conform to the contract, the illustration recognises the cost of making them conform.

learningObjectives: Identify the statutory routes to compensation under Section 73.
Distinguish recoverable loss from remote or indirect loss using the statutory wording and illustrations.
Apply the Explanation concerning means available to remedy the inconvenience caused by non-performance.
Organise evidence and quantify each claimed head of loss without inventing authority.
enhancement.definition: Section 73 is the statutory rule for compensation for loss or damage caused by breach of contract and for failure to discharge an obligation resembling one created by contract.
enhancement.legalPrinciple: Compensation is available for loss that naturally arose in the usual course of things or was of a kind the parties knew at contract formation was likely to result; remote and indirect loss is excluded, and available means of remedying the inconvenience must be taken into account when estimating loss.
statutoryFramework: Indian Contract Act, 1872 — Section 73, including the Explanation and statutory illustrations
Related statutory provisions: Sections 74 and 75 (distinct bases for relief)
essentialIngredients: Identify the contract or obligation resembling one created by contract
Establish breach or failure to discharge the obligation
Show loss or damage caused by that breach/failure
Connect each head of loss to the natural-course limb or the parties' knowledge-at-formation limb
Account for means available to remedy the inconvenience when estimating loss
enhancement.detailedExplanation: Section 73 has two stated routes for loss caused by breach: loss that naturally arose in the usual course of things, and loss of a kind the parties knew when making the contract was likely to result. The section excludes remote and indirect loss. Its Explanation requires the means that existed to remedy the inconvenience caused by non-performance to be taken into account when estimating loss. The statutory illustrations give fact-specific examples, including market difference for undelivered goods, expense of substitute carriage, repair costs for defective work and a limit on a downstream contract loss that had not been communicated to the supplier. The application remains fact-sensitive; each claimed amount needs a supported causal link and evidence.
examples: Market difference for undelivered goods: The Act illustrates a seller who fails to deliver goods. The buyer's measure is the amount, if any, by which the contract price falls short of the price for which goods of like quality could have been obtained at the relevant delivery time.

Substitute carriage and avoidable inconvenience: The Act illustrates a ship that does not arrive for a planned cargo. If the other party obtains suitable alternative conveyance on equally advantageous terms but incurs trouble and expense, the illustration allows compensation for that trouble and expense.

Uncommunicated downstream contract: The Act illustrates a machinery delivery breach where the buyer also loses a third-party contract that had not been communicated to the supplier when contracting. The illustration distinguishes the replacement-cost difference from the downstream compensation paid to the third party.
Defective repair work: The Act illustrates repairs performed contrary to the contract. The stated measure is the cost of making the repairs conform to the contract.
problemApplication: List each claimed head of loss separately and identify the contractual breach or undischarged contract-like obligation.
For each head, apply the natural-course limb or the knowledge-at-formation limb, with facts and evidence.
Test whether the loss is remote or indirect and explain why.
Identify available means of remedying the inconvenience and account for them in the estimate.
Quantify the supported amount and distinguish any claim governed by Sections 74 or 75.
keyTakeaways: Section 73 permits compensation for loss that naturally arose in the usual course or was known by the parties at contract formation to be likely to result.
Remote and indirect loss is excluded.
The statutory Explanation requires available means of remedying the inconvenience to be considered when estimating loss.
The statutory illustrations are fact-specific and should not be treated as automatic outcomes for materially different facts.
No case-law verification is claimed in this update.

distinctions: Section 73 concerns compensation measured by loss caused by breach or failure to discharge a contract-like obligation; Section 74 separately addresses a stipulated sum or penalty for breach.
Section 75 concerns compensation for damage sustained through non-fulfilment where a person rightfully rescinds a contract.
The natural-course limb and the parties'-knowledge-at-formation limb are alternative statutory routes; do not assume every special or downstream loss is recoverable.
The statutory Explanation requires consideration of available means to remedy the inconvenience when estimating loss.
